meta.title: Who really said "You are all a lost generation"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Gertrude Stein is credited with it, but the words survive only through Hemingway's The Sun Also Rises (1926) epigraph — and Stein said the phrase wasn't even hers.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You are all a lost generation'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Gertrude Stein, the line survives through Hemingway's 1926 epigraph — and Stein said she borrowed the phrase from a French garage owner.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Credibly and widely credited to Stein as something she said in conversation: Ernest Hemingway printed it as the epigraph to The Sun Also Rises (1926), attributed to “Gertrude Stein in conversation,” and retold the exchange in A Moveable Feast (1964). But no text in Stein’s own hand contains the exact line, and Stein herself said the phrase originated with someone else — so the wording is best called attributed, not verified.

source.heading: The source

source.excerpt:
You are all a lost generation.
— Gertrude Stein in conversation
trail: Hemingway printed the line as the epigraph of The Sun Also Rises (1926), reading “You are all a lost generation. — Gertrude Stein in conversation” (Standard Ebooks).

Quote Investigator documents that the phrase did not originate with Stein: Hemingway’s 1925 account credits a French garage owner in the Department of Ain, while Stein’s 1937 Everybody’s Autobiography credits a hotel keeper.
Wikiquote lists the remark as a genuine Stein statement, sourced to Hemingway’s A Moveable Feast (1964) and the Sun Also Rises epigraph rather than to any text Stein published herself.
source.excerptNote: The wording as Hemingway printed it on the epigraph page of The Sun Also Rises (1926). Hemingway later described the scene in A Moveable Feast, where Stein delivers the line about young people who had served in the war.

source.rightsNote: The exact wording first reached print as the epigraph to Hemingway’s The Sun Also Rises (1926), which entered the U.S. public domain on 1 January 2022. Hemingway’s fuller retelling of the conversation in A Moveable Feast (1964) remains in copyright (Hemingway estate / Scribner).

author.name: Gertrude Stein
author.heading: About Gertrude Stein
author.metaLine: 1874–1946 · American writer, poet & Paris salon host
author.bio: Gertrude Stein was an American writer and art collector whose Paris apartment at 27 rue de Fleurus became a hub for modernist writers and painters. She mentored and sparred with the young Ernest Hemingway, who credited her with the phrase that came to name a generation. Stein always maintained she had picked the words up from a French tradesman rather than coining them herself.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The line is genuinely tied to Stein — but two popular beliefs about it are shakier than the confident retellings suggest.

items.why: Stein is routinely credited with coining the phrase, but she explicitly attributed it to someone else. Per Quote Investigator, Hemingway’s 1925 account credits a garage owner in France’s Department of Ain, and Stein’s own 1937 Everybody’s Autobiography credits a hotel keeper.

There is no Stein-authored text containing “You are all a lost generation.” The wording survives only through Hemingway, who framed it as the Sun Also Rises epigraph “in conversation” and dramatized it in A Moveable Feast nearly four decades later.

misattribution.truthLine: Stein really did say something to this effect — but she borrowed the phrase, and the polished wording we quote is Hemingway’s, first fixed in print as his 1926 epigraph (Quote Investigator).

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The single sentence gave a name to the writers and veterans who came of age during the First World War — Hemingway, Fitzgerald, and their circle — and it did so before the reader reached the first page of The Sun Also Rises. Hemingway set Stein’s remark against a passage from Ecclesiastes, so the book opens by weighing a generation’s disillusion against the endurance of the earth.
Hemingway’s own feelings about the label were mixed: in A Moveable Feast he recalled resisting it even as he made it famous, which is part of why the phrase carries both Stein’s voice and his.
context.pull: A name for a generation, borrowed from a garage, sharpened by Hemingway, and pinned forever on Stein.
